name: SAM.gov
purpose: Official US system for award management: entity registrations for organisations doing business with the federal government, contract opportunities, exclusions (debarment) and assistance listings, with APIs and bulk extracts.
journalism_use_case: Resolving who a surveillance supplier actually is: the entity registration gives legal name, address, ownership and business-size declarations, which is how you connect a contract award to a corporate structure — and the exclusions list tells you whether a vendor has been debarred.
pros: Entity registration data links a contracting name to a legal entity with an address and identifiers, which is the bridge between procurement records and corporate-registry research
Contract-opportunity notices show what agencies are about to buy, so you can report a surveillance procurement before it is awarded — considerably more valuable than reporting it afterwards
Exclusions (debarment) records are a direct accountability signal about a vendor's standing
Free, official and API-accessible, so monitoring is possible rather than only searching
cons: Registration and API access increasingly require accounts and, for some data, approval — which creates a record of your interest and can be a barrier for a non-US organisation
The interface is bureaucratic and the data model (UEI, CAGE codes, NAICS) takes learning before queries are productive
Self-declared registration data, so ownership and business-size declarations are the vendor's own claims and need verification against registries
US only, and the ownership detail is thinner than a proper corporate registry — it identifies the entity rather than mapping its structure
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: sam.gov verified live on 2026-11-17 (200). SAM.gov is the mandatory registration system for US federal contractors, which is what makes its entity data authoritative for that purpose.
assessment: Use it as the entity-resolution layer alongside USAspending rather than as a standalone source — USAspending tells you what was bought, SAM.gov tells you who the seller legally is, and together they support a nameable story. For your profile the opportunity notices are the underused half: a standing watch on relevant NAICS and keyword terms surfaces surveillance procurement at the solicitation stage, which is both earlier and more newsworthy than an award.
maintenance_evidence: Portal verified live on 2026-11-17 (200). A mandatory statutory US government system under continuous operation; maintenance is institutional.
licence: US federal government works are generally not subject to copyright in the United States; portal terms and API usage conditions NOT verified in this survey
licence_restrictions: Not verified here. API access conditions and any registration requirements should be checked before building a monitoring pipeline.
costs: Free. API access may require registration. Infrastructure only if you build monitoring. Estimate.
privacy: Public records about organisations. Registering for API access creates an identifiable account, which discloses your organisation's interest — consider how that account is attributed.
alternatives: USAspending for the award data itself
State corporate registries and OpenCorporates for genuine ownership structure
FPDS for the raw federal procurement feed
blockers: Some data and API access require registration, creating a record of your interest

name: US Senate Lobbying Disclosure Act database
maintainer: US Senate Office of Public Records
purpose: Official searchable database of lobbying registrations and quarterly activity reports filed under the US Lobbying Disclosure Act, naming clients, registrants, lobbyists, issues and expenditures.
journalism_use_case: Showing that a surveillance vendor lobbied a specific agency or on specific legislation: LDA filings name the client, the issues and often the agencies contacted, which is documentary evidence of an attempt to shape policy — the political half of a surveillance-industry story that procurement records cannot provide.
pros: Primary official filings rather than a secondary compilation, so the record is citable and the vendor cannot dispute its own filing
Issue descriptions and agency contacts reveal what a vendor wanted, which is frequently more revealing than the amount spent
Quarterly cadence means a time series is available, so you can show lobbying intensifying around a procurement or a legislative moment
Free and public with bulk data available
cons: The portal returned 403 to automated requests in this survey, which is bot protection rather than unavailability — but it means scripted collection needs care and may be blocked, so plan on manual or carefully-rate-limited access
Filings are self-reported with broad issue descriptions, so a filing establishes that lobbying occurred without revealing what was said
Coverage is federal US only, and much surveillance-policy influence occurs through channels that do not trigger LDA registration (trade associations, conferences, informal contact)
Entity naming is inconsistent across filings, so aggregating a vendor's activity requires name normalisation
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the portal returned HTTP 403 to curl on 2026-11-17 — recorded in sources/evidence/b2-sources.md as bot protection rather than evidence of removal, since a 403 says nothing about whether the resource exists. Verify in a browser before concluding anything about availability.
assessment: Use it, with the honest caveat that this survey could not fully verify its current interface because of bot protection — check it in a browser before planning a pipeline. For your profile the analytically strongest use is correlation: lobbying filings by a vendor, plotted against procurement awards and legislative milestones, make a case about influence that neither dataset supports alone. OpenSecrets provides a cleaned, aggregated view that is easier to work with, at the cost of being secondary.
maintenance_evidence: Not verifiable by automated request in this survey: the portal returned HTTP 403 to curl on 2026-11-17, which is consistent with bot protection on a live service rather than with removal. Classified Uncertain for honesty — the service is a statutory obligation and almost certainly operating, but I did not confirm it.
licence: US government records; specific reuse terms NOT verified in this survey
licence_restrictions: Not verified. US government records are generally freely reusable; confirm before publishing bulk extracts.
costs: Free. Cost is collection effort given bot protection, plus name normalisation.
privacy: Public filings about organisations and named lobbyists. Your searches are visible to the portal.
alternatives: OpenSecrets for a cleaned, aggregated and more analysable view of the same filings
House of Representatives lobbying disclosures for the other chamber's filings
EU Transparency Register for the European equivalent — though its current entry point is unresolved, see the evidence note
blockers: Bot protection blocks automated collection; current interface not verified in this survey

name: OpenSecrets lobbying data
maintainer: OpenSecrets (Center for Responsive Politics / Issue One)
purpose: Cleaned, standardised and aggregated database of US federal lobbying and campaign-finance data built from official filings, with organisation profiles, issue breakdowns and an API.
journalism_use_case: The analysable version of US lobbying records: instead of reconciling inconsistent filing names yourself, you get a vendor's lobbying history aggregated under one organisation profile — which turns a week of data cleaning into an afternoon's analysis when reporting on a surveillance company's political spending.
pros: Entity standardisation is the real product: OpenSecrets has already solved the name-matching problem that makes raw LDA data painful, and that is most of the work
Organisation profiles combine lobbying with campaign-finance data, giving a fuller picture of a vendor's political activity than either dataset alone
Long-established non-profit with a research mission, so the methodology is documented and the data is intended for exactly this use
API access makes systematic analysis possible rather than page-by-page reading
cons: Secondary source: it is a cleaned derivative of official filings, so for a contested claim you should cite the underlying LDA filing and use OpenSecrets to find it
The site returned 403 to automated requests in this survey (bot protection, not removal), so scripted access needs the API rather than scraping, and API terms were not verified here
US federal focus, with state-level coverage thinner — so non-US and subnational surveillance-lobbying questions are out of scope
Aggregation decisions (which subsidiaries roll up to which parent) are OpenSecrets' editorial choices, and they matter for the numbers you publish
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the federal-lobbying page returned HTTP 403 to curl on 2026-11-17, recorded as bot protection rather than unavailability. OpenSecrets data is extensively used in US political journalism, which is well established.
assessment: Use it to find and frame, then cite the primary filing — that is the right division between a cleaned aggregate and an official record. For your profile the practical note is that the aggregation decisions are consequential: if you publish 'the company spent X on lobbying', check whether that figure includes subsidiaries and say so. Verify the current API terms before building anything, since this survey could not.
maintenance_evidence: Not confirmable by automated request (HTTP 403 to curl on 2026-11-17, consistent with bot protection on a live site). OpenSecrets is a long-operating research organisation publishing continuously; classification rests on that institutional record rather than on a verified fetch, hence medium confidence.
licence: OpenSecrets data terms apply and were NOT verified in this survey — historically permitting non-commercial research use with attribution and requiring permission for bulk or commercial reuse
model_or_data_licence: Same. Verify terms before republishing data or building a product.
licence_restrictions: Not verified here, and this matters: a research organisation's data terms commonly restrict bulk and commercial reuse, so a commercially operated newsroom should confirm its position before republishing OpenSecrets data as a dataset.
costs: Free to read. API access and bulk data terms not verified in this survey; historically free for research use with registration. Confirm before planning.
privacy: Public records about organisations and individuals in political activity. Your queries are visible to OpenSecrets.
alternatives: Senate LDA database for the primary filings you should cite
LobbyFacts or EU Transparency Register data for European lobbying
Direct FOI requests to agencies for meeting records, which reveal contact that lobbying filings summarise
blockers: Data reuse terms not verified — confirm before republishing as a dataset

name: Open Contracting Data Standard
purpose: Open data standard for publishing structured information about public contracting across the whole process — planning, tender, award, contract and implementation — with schemas, extensions and validation tooling.
journalism_use_case: The common format that makes cross-country procurement analysis possible: where governments publish OCDS data, you can compare surveillance purchases across jurisdictions using one schema instead of writing a parser per country. It also defines the fields to demand when a government's procurement data is unusable.
pros: Standardisation is the enabling condition for comparative procurement journalism, and OCDS is the standard that has actually been adopted by a meaningful number of governments
Covers the full contracting lifecycle including planning and implementation, so you can report on modifications and overruns rather than only awards — where surveillance contracts often grow quietly
Validation tooling and extensions mean you can check a government's published data against the standard and demonstrate where it is deficient, which is itself a story
Open standard with public schemas and an institutional steward, so it is a durable reference rather than a vendor format
cons: A standard, not a dataset: its usefulness depends entirely on whether the governments you cover publish in it, and adoption is uneven — many do not
Publishers implement partially, so OCDS-labelled data frequently omits the fields you most want (supplier identifiers, contract documents, modifications)
Session 1's recorded URL (standards.open-contracting.org) did not respond in this survey; the working entry point is open-contracting.org/data-standard/ (verified 2026-11-17)
Engineer-facing: working with OCDS data means schema work, and the pay-off only arrives when several publishers are compared
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the session-1 URL did not respond while open-contracting.org/data-standard/ returned 200 (both checked 2026-11-17, recorded in sources/evidence/b2-sources.md). OCDS adoption by national procurement authorities is documented by the Open Contracting Partnership.
assessment: Integrate it where your jurisdictions publish OCDS — it removes the per-country parser problem that otherwise makes comparative procurement work prohibitive. For your profile there is a second, advocacy-adjacent use worth knowing: validating a government's procurement publication against the standard produces a concrete, citable account of what it conceals, which is a reportable finding in its own right and a strong basis for a transparency request.
maintenance_evidence: Standard documentation verified live on 2026-11-17 (open-contracting.org/data-standard/ returns 200); the standard repository and its schema versioning are maintained by the Open Contracting Partnership with a published versioning policy. Maintenance here means schema and extension governance rather than software releases.
licence: Apache-2.0 for the standard and schemas (confirm the repository licence file for your records)
model_or_data_licence: Published OCDS datasets carry each publisher's own licence, which varies by government and must be checked per source.
licence_restrictions: The standard is openly licensed. The data is the variable: individual publishers' licences differ and some restrict reuse, so check per jurisdiction before republishing.
costs: No fee. Engineer time for schema work; negligible infrastructure.
privacy: A standard and public datasets about public bodies; no privacy dimension beyond ordinary web access.
alternatives: TED for EU procurement in its own format
National procurement portals directly, accepting per-country parsing
OpenCorporates or national registries to resolve supplier identities that OCDS data often leaves ambiguous
blockers: Value depends on publisher adoption, which is uneven and often partial

name: OpenCellID
purpose: Crowdsourced database of cell-tower locations and identifiers (MCC, MNC, LAC, cell ID) worldwide, with an API and bulk downloads for looking up or reverse-looking-up cell identifiers.
journalism_use_case: Two uses in surveillance work: corroborating Rayhunter or SnoopSnitch anomalies against known tower infrastructure to distinguish a legitimate cell from a suspected simulator, and resolving cell identifiers found in device records or leaked location data into physical locations.
pros: Provides the reference layer that makes cell-site anomaly detection interpretable: an unknown cell ID at a location where no tower is recorded is a meaningful signal, and without a reference database it is just noise
Bulk downloads allow offline lookup, which matters both for privacy and for field use without connectivity
Global crowdsourced coverage means it reaches places commercial datasets neglect
Documentation is clear and the API is straightforward to integrate
cons: Crowdsourced coverage is uneven and ages: a genuine new tower may be absent, producing a false 'unknown cell' signal — so absence from OpenCellID is weak evidence of a simulator and must not be reported as detection
Operated by a commercial company (Unwired Labs), and access terms including any free-tier limits were NOT verified in this survey — treat as unknown pending a check
Position estimates are derived from crowdsourced observations, so tower locations carry error that matters when you are reasoning about coverage areas
Queries disclose which cell identifiers and areas you are investigating to the operator
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: docs.opencellid.org verified live on 2026-11-17 (200). The database's crowdsourced nature and the resulting coverage variability are documented characteristics rather than criticisms.
assessment: Integrate it as the reference layer behind any cellular-surveillance work, with the limitation stated explicitly in anything you publish: an unrecorded cell is not evidence of an IMSI catcher, because the database is incomplete. For your profile the practical approach is to download bulk data for your regions of interest so lookups are offline and private, and to treat OpenCellID agreement as corroboration while treating disagreement as a question rather than a finding. Verify the access terms before building a dependency.
maintenance_evidence: Documentation site verified live on 2026-11-17 (200), but this survey did not verify current access terms, free-tier limits or data-update cadence. The database is crowdsourced and commercially operated; classified Uncertain because continuity and terms for a commercially operated community dataset cannot be assessed from a documentation fetch alone.
licence: Not verified in this survey — OpenCellID has historically offered data under a Creative Commons licence with API access tiers operated by Unwired Labs; confirm current terms before use
licence_restrictions: Unverified and material: a CC-BY-SA-style licence would impose share-alike obligations on a derived dataset, and commercial API terms may restrict redistribution. Confirm before publishing derived data.
costs: Not verified in this survey. Historically a free tier with API keys and paid tiers above it; confirm current pricing before planning. No software cost.
privacy: API queries disclose the cell identifiers and areas you are investigating to the operator. Bulk download and offline lookup avoids this entirely and is the configuration to prefer for sensitive work.
alternatives: National regulator tower registries where published, which are authoritative rather than crowdsourced
Mozilla Location Service-style datasets where still available
Rayhunter's own anomaly analysis without external corroboration, accepting weaker conclusions
blockers: Licence and access terms unverified; crowdsourced coverage gaps mean an unknown cell is not evidence of a simulator

name: Citizen Lab publication directory
maintainer: Citizen Lab (Munk School, University of Toronto)
purpose: Searchable directory of Citizen Lab's published research on targeted surveillance, censorship, spyware vendors and information controls, with full reports and technical indicators.
journalism_use_case: The reference corpus for surveillance-industry reporting: before investigating a vendor, read what Citizen Lab has already established about its infrastructure, customers and targeting patterns — which saves duplicating forensic work and provides citable attribution that a newsroom usually cannot produce itself.
pros: The most authoritative open body of research on commercial spyware and its deployment against journalists, with technical depth no newsroom can replicate in-house
Reports include infrastructure indicators and methodology, so they are usable as both background and a starting point for your own verification
Citable academic provenance, which materially strengthens a published claim about a vendor's conduct
Free and publicly accessible, with the directory verified live in this survey
cons: Not a tool or a dataset you can query programmatically — it is a publication archive, so systematic use means reading rather than analysis
Coverage follows Citizen Lab's research priorities, which are extensive but not comprehensive: absence of a vendor from the directory means nothing about that vendor
Findings are point-in-time: a vendor's infrastructure and customer list change after publication, so an indicator from a 2023 report may be stale
Reproducing or extending their technical findings requires forensic capability (MVT-class work) that most newsrooms will need a partner for
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the publication directory was verified live on 2026-11-17 (200). Citizen Lab's research is extensively cited in journalism and litigation concerning commercial spyware, which is the relevant evidence of its standing.
assessment: Treat it as required reading rather than tooling — and as the route to a partnership. For your profile the highest-value action is not consuming the reports but building a relationship: Citizen Lab, Amnesty Security Lab and Access Now have forensic capability your newsroom will not, and surveillance stories involving journalist targeting typically require exactly that. Read the directory to know what is established, then bring them what you find.
maintenance_evidence: Directory verified live on 2026-11-17 (200). An actively publishing academic research group; maintenance means continued publication rather than software releases, and the research output is continuous and public.
licence: Citizen Lab publications are generally released under Creative Commons terms; specific per-report licences NOT verified in this survey
model_or_data_licence: Same. Technical indicators published alongside reports carry the report's terms.
licence_restrictions: Not verified per report. Quoting and citing research is ordinary journalistic use; republishing reports or indicator sets wholesale requires checking the specific licence.
privacy: Reading a public research archive. Your browsing is visible to the host in the ordinary way; use Tor if your interest in a specific vendor is itself sensitive.
alternatives: Amnesty Security Lab publications and indicators for overlapping coverage
Privacy International's research and litigation records on the surveillance industry
Direct partnership with a forensic lab for original technical work
